passages.happening: “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ: Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you” (verses 1-2).
passages.hearers:
The writer names himself Jude, the Greek form of the name Judah. He calls himself ‘a brother of James’. The James he names without explaining is almost certainly James the brother of Jesus, who led the church in Jerusalem. So Jude was most likely a brother of Jesus too; Mark lists a Judas among Jesus' brothers (Mark 6:3). Like James, he did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), and came to faith later.

Yet he does not call himself ‘the brother of the Lord’. He calls himself ‘a servant of Jesus Christ’. Many readers see humility in that. Family ties to Jesus mattered less to Jude than serving him.

Then he describes his readers in three words. They are ‘called’: God has invited them. They are ‘loved by God the Father’. And they are ‘kept in Jesus Christ’, guarded by him. That last word, kept, will come back at the end of the letter. Jude is about to write hard things about people who fall. He begins by telling his readers that they are held.

His greeting is also in threes: mercy, peace and love, ‘multiplied’, given more and more.
passages.ot:
‘Called’ and ‘loved’ are words God spoke over Israel: “I have called you by your name; you are Mine” (Isaiah 43:1). And “I have loved you with an everlasting love” (Jeremiah 31:3).

‘Kept’ is the psalm's promise: “The LORD will watch over your coming and going, both now and forevermore” (Psalm 121:8).
passages.asks: Ask whether you think of yourself first as called, loved and kept, or first by your failures. Ask whether you, like Jude, would rather be known as Christ's servant than for any connection you have. And ask whom you could wish mercy, peace and love today.

passages.happening:
“Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (verse 3).

“For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Jude had planned a different letter, a warm one about ‘the salvation we share’. Something forced him to change.

He asks his readers to ‘contend earnestly’ for the faith. The word comes from athletic contests: a hard, determined struggle. It appears only here in the New Testament. Jude is not calling for violence. He is calling for a refusal to give the faith away.

‘The faith entrusted once for all to the saints’ is a body of teaching handed down, not invented. The church does not rewrite it to suit its appetites. It guards it and passes it on.

Then the reason. ‘Certain men have crept in among you unnoticed.’ The danger was inside the church, not outside. They had slipped in quietly. And Jude names two things they did.

They turned grace into licence. The grace of God, which forgives sinners, became for them a reason to sin freely. And they denied ‘our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ’. The word for Master, despotēs, is a word often used of God.

‘Designated long ago for condemnation’ means that Scripture had long spoken of such people and their end. Jude is about to show where.
passages.ot:
The prophets saw false teachers who made sin easy: “They dress the wound of My people with very little care, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there is no peace at all” (Jeremiah 6:14).

And they warned against those who call evil good: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20).
passages.hard:
‘Contend earnestly for the faith.’ Does this give Christians permission to be harsh with anyone who disagrees with them?

No. Jude's fierce words are about people who were turning God's grace into a cover for immorality and denying Christ. They are not about every person a believer disagrees with, or every question on which faithful Christians differ.

And Jude's own letter shows what contending looks like. It means knowing and keeping the faith that was handed down. It means building one another up, praying, and keeping oneself in God's love. And it ends with mercy for those who doubt (verses 20-23). Contending for the faith never cancels compassion for people.
passages.asks: Ask what ‘the faith entrusted once for all’ means to you, and whether you know it well enough to keep it. Ask whether you have ever treated God's grace as permission. And ask how you can stand firm without becoming harsh.

passages.happening:
“Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe” (verse 5).

“And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day” (verse 6).

“In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Jude assumes his readers know these stories well. He only needs to remind them.

First, Israel. God rescued his people from Egypt, but afterward those who would not believe died in the wilderness. Being rescued once did not mean they could not fall. In verse 5 the old copies differ. Several early and important manuscripts say ‘Jesus’ delivered his people out of Egypt, and the BSB follows them. Others read ‘the Lord’ or ‘God’. If ‘Jesus’ is the original reading, Jude names Christ as the God who acted in Israel's history.

Second, the angels. They ‘did not stay within their own domain’. They left the place God gave them, and they are now held for judgment. Notice the word play. They did not keep their place, so God keeps them in chains.

Third, Sodom and Gomorrah, destroyed by fire in Abraham's day. They are ‘on display as an example’.

The three examples have one point. God's patience is not indifference. Those who were inside God's people, who had seen his rescue, are not exempt from his judgment.
passages.ot:
The wilderness story is in Numbers. The LORD said, “How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them?” (Numbers 14:11). “Your bodies will fall in this wilderness” (Numbers 14:29).

Behind the angels many readers see Genesis 6: “the sons of God saw that the daughters of men were beautiful, and they took as wives whomever they chose” (Genesis 6:2).

And Sodom: “Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah—from the LORD out of the heavens” (Genesis 19:24). The prophets used Sodom as a warning ever after: “Some of you I overthrew as I overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah” (Amos 4:11).
passages.hard:
Who are the angels of verse 6? And how should verse 7, about Sodom and ‘strange flesh’, be read?

On the angels, many readers think Jude means the ‘sons of God’ of Genesis 6:1-4, read as heavenly beings, as the book of 1 Enoch read them: watchers who took human wives and were imprisoned in darkness until judgment. Others read Genesis 6 differently, as the family of Seth or as powerful kings, as the notes on Genesis 6 set out, and so take Jude more generally, of angels who rebelled. These notes do not choose. 2 Peter 2:4 speaks of the same angels in other words.

On verse 7, Christians read it in more than one way, as they read Genesis 19. All agree that the men of Sodom tried to rape two strangers, and that this was monstrous. The traditional reading, held by most churches through history, sees the same-sex nature of the demand as part of what Jude condemns, along with the violence. Its holders point to Leviticus 18:22. Another reading holds that the point is violent cruelty to strangers, and notes that Jude's ‘strange flesh’ (in Greek, ‘other flesh’) has been read by some as the angels, since the visitors to Sodom were angels (Genesis 19:1). These notes take no side on that question here. On both readings nothing in this verse gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.

If you are gay, or love someone who is, you are met with respect here. If these verses weigh on you, talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask whether you have ever assumed that being rescued once means you can live as you like. Ask what these old examples say about God's patience. And ask whether you read hard verses in a way that leaves room for contempt, or in a way that leaves you humble.

passages.happening:
“Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings. But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you!’ These men, however, slander what they do not understand, and like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively” (verses 8-10).

“Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion” (verse 11).

“These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted. They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever” (verses 12-13).
passages.hearers:
Now Jude turns to the intruders, and again and again he says ‘these men’. They are ‘dreamers’, perhaps claiming visions as their authority. They defile their bodies, reject authority, and speak with contempt about heavenly beings they do not understand.

Then a surprising story. Even the archangel Michael, the great angel who appears in Daniel, did not hurl insults at the devil when they disputed over Moses' body. He left the judgment to God: “The Lord rebuke you!” The story is not in the Old Testament. Early Christian writers, including Origen, said it came from a work known as the Assumption of Moses (see below).

Then three figures from Israel's story, each a warning. Cain, who killed his brother in envy. Balaam, the prophet who went for money. Korah, who rebelled against the leaders God had given. By Jude's day these three had become stock examples of envy, greed and rebellion.

Then a rush of pictures. ‘Hidden reefs’ at the church's love feasts, the shared meals where the rich fed the poor, often with the Lord's Supper: rocks under the water that wreck ships. Some translate the word ‘stains’ instead. ‘Shepherding only themselves’: leaders who feed on the flock. Clouds that promise rain and give none. Trees with no fruit even at harvest, dead at the root. Wild waves throwing up foam. And ‘wandering stars’. Ancient sailors and travellers steered by the stars. A star that wandered off course was no use as a guide.

Each picture says the same thing. These people promise much and give nothing, and they are dangerous because they look like part of the church.
passages.ot:
Jude's three figures come from Genesis and Numbers. Cain: “So Cain became very angry, and his countenance fell” (Genesis 4:5). Balaam: “The elders of Moab and Midian departed with the fees for divination in hand” (Numbers 22:7). Korah, who with others “conducted a rebellion against Moses” (Numbers 16:1-2).

Michael appears in Daniel: “Then Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me” (Daniel 10:13). His words echo the prophet: “The LORD rebukes you, Satan” (Zechariah 3:2).

Moses' burial is told in Deuteronomy: “no one to this day knows the location of his grave” (Deuteronomy 34:6).

And the pictures come from the prophets and wisdom books: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel, who only feed themselves” (Ezekiel 34:2). “But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck” (Isaiah 57:20). “Like clouds and wind without rain is the man who boasts of gifts never given” (Proverbs 25:14).
passages.hard:
Where does the story of Michael and Moses' body come from? Is it Scripture?

Deuteronomy says only that God buried Moses and that no one knows where his grave is. The story of Michael disputing with the devil over the body is not in the Old Testament. Early Christian writers, including Origen, said Jude took it from a work known as the Assumption of Moses. A related text, known as the Testament of Moses, survives in part, but its ending is lost, so the passage Jude drew on cannot now be checked.

Using a story his readers knew does not make every part of that book Scripture. Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) and a Jewish tradition about Jannes and Jambres (2 Timothy 3:8) without treating those sources as Scripture. Jude uses the story for one point: even the greatest angel left judgment to God. The note on verses 14-16 says more about books outside the Bible.
passages.asks: Ask whether you, like Michael, leave final judgment to God, or whether you are quick to pronounce it. Ask which of the pictures, waterless clouds, fruitless trees, wandering stars, would describe a faith that looks good but gives nothing. And ask whether you look after others, or only yourself.

passages.happening: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: ‘Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners.’ These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts; their mouths spew arrogance; they flatter others for their own advantage” (verses 14-16).
passages.hearers:
Jude quotes a prophecy of Enoch. Enoch is the man of Genesis 5 who ‘walked with God’, the seventh in the line from Adam. The words Jude quotes closely match a passage in a book called 1 Enoch (1:9).

1 Enoch is a collection of Jewish writings named after this Enoch, written over the last centuries before Christ. Fragments of it in Aramaic were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Many Jews in Jude's day read it and valued it. Jude's readers would have known it.

The prophecy is about the Lord coming in judgment, with ‘myriads of His holy ones’, a huge host. Notice how often ‘ungodly’ comes: four times. The judgment falls on ungodly deeds and on harsh words spoken against God.

Then Jude applies it, again with ‘these men’. They grumble. They follow their own desires. They boast. And they flatter people to get what they want.
passages.ot:
Enoch appears in Genesis: “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away” (Genesis 5:24).

The coming of the Lord with his holy ones is an Old Testament picture too. In Moses' blessing, “The LORD came from Sinai and dawned upon us from Seir; He shone forth from Mount Paran and came with myriads of holy ones” (Deuteronomy 33:2). And Zechariah: “Then the LORD my God will come, and all the holy ones with Him” (Zechariah 14:5).

The grumbling recalls Israel in the wilderness: “because you have grumbled against Me” (Numbers 14:29).
passages.hard:
Jude quotes 1 Enoch. Does that make 1 Enoch Scripture?

This troubled some in the early church. Jerome, late in the 300s, noted that many rejected Jude for that reason. Others, including Tertullian, argued that Jude's use of Enoch showed the book had value.

Christians have generally answered in one of several ways. Many say that quoting a book is not the same as calling it Scripture, just as Paul quotes Greek poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12) without making them Scripture. On this view, Jude affirms that this one saying is a true prophecy of the Lord's coming, which agrees with the Old Testament, without making the rest of 1 Enoch Scripture. Others note that Jude was writing to readers who valued these works, and used them as common ground. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, by contrast, includes 1 Enoch in its Bible, and has done so to this day.

For most churches, Jude's use of 1 Enoch shows how deeply the first Christians lived in the Jewish world of their day. It is not a reason to add the book to the Bible, and it is not a reason to doubt Jude. These notes do not go beyond what Jude himself does: he quotes one saying, and calls it prophecy.
passages.asks: Ask what it means to you that the Lord is coming, and whether that is a comfort or a fear. Ask whether you grumble, boast or flatter to get your way. And ask how you read books outside the Bible: with interest, with care, and with Scripture as the measure.

passages.happening:
“But you, beloved, remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ when they said to you, ‘In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.’ These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit” (verses 17-19).

“But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life” (verses 20-21).

“And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh” (verses 22-23).
passages.hearers:
Twice Jude turns with ‘But you, beloved’. After all the warnings, he speaks to the faithful.

First, remember. The apostles had warned that scoffers would come. This trouble was not a sign that the faith had failed. It had been foretold. Some scholars read verse 17 as looking back on the apostles from a distance, one of their reasons for thinking the letter was written later; the book page sets out both views.

The scoffers ‘cause divisions’, and they are ‘devoid of the Spirit’. The intruders may have claimed to be the truly spiritual ones. Jude says they are the ones without the Spirit.

Then four things to do. Build yourselves up in the faith. Pray in the Holy Spirit. Keep yourselves in the love of God. And wait for the mercy of Jesus Christ. Notice that the readers are told to ‘keep yourselves’. At the start Jude said they are ‘kept in Jesus Christ’ (verse 1), and at the end he will praise the God who is ‘able to keep you’ (verse 24). God keeps them, and they keep themselves in his love. The two stand side by side.

And then, last of all, mercy. Not for the intruders' teaching, but for people. Those who doubt are to be met with mercy, not suspicion. Some need to be pulled from danger, ‘snatched from the fire’. Others need mercy with care, so that the helper is not drawn into the same sin. ‘Hating even the clothing stained by the flesh’ is a strong picture: love the person, and hate the sin that clings.
passages.ot:
‘Snatching them from the fire’ comes from the prophets. The LORD says of the high priest Joshua, “Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?” (Zechariah 3:2).

‘Stained clothing’ comes from the same vision, where Joshua stood before the angel in filthy garments, and the angel said, “Take off his filthy clothes” (Zechariah 3:4).

And keeping oneself in God's love is the psalm's longing: “But as for me, it is good to draw near to God” (Psalm 73:28).
passages.hard:
‘Have mercy on those who doubt.’ What does this say to Christians who have doubts?

It says that doubt is not the same as the rebellion Jude has been describing. The intruders turned grace into licence and denied Christ. Those who doubt are people inside the church who are struggling. Jude's instruction is to meet them with mercy.

That is a word for churches. People with honest questions should find patience and help, not suspicion. And it is a word for anyone who doubts. You are not one of the ‘these men’ of this letter because you have questions. The site's Honest Answers take up many of the questions people ask.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Ask what you do to build yourself up in the faith, and whether you pray. Ask whom you know who doubts, and whether you have shown them mercy or suspicion. And ask whom you could help pull back from danger, with care.

passages.t: To him who is able to keep you
passages.happening: “Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy— to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen” (verses 24-25).
passages.hearers:
The letter ends with a doxology, a prayer of praise. It is one of the most loved in the New Testament, and churches have prayed it and sung it ever since.

After all Jude's warnings about people who fall, his last word is about the God who keeps. He ‘is able to keep you from stumbling’. The faithful do not hold themselves up by their own grip. They are held by one who is able.

And there is more. God will ‘present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy’. The picture is of being brought before a king, spotless, and the joy is great.

The praise goes to ‘the only God our Savior’, through Jesus Christ our Lord. And it reaches across all time: ‘before all time, and now, and for all eternity’.
passages.ot:
The psalms praise the God who keeps his people's feet: “He will not allow your foot to slip; your Protector will not slumber” (Psalm 121:3). And “He preserves our lives and keeps our feet from slipping” (Psalm 66:9).

Israel confessed God as the only Saviour: “I, yes I, am the LORD, and there is no Savior but Me” (Isaiah 43:11).

And the hope of standing before God with joy is the psalm's too: “You will fill me with joy in Your presence” (Psalm 16:11).
passages.asks: Ask whether you trust God to keep you, or whether you try to hold yourself up alone. Ask what it would mean to stand before God ‘with great joy’. And pray these two verses, for yourself and for someone you love.
